Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
You can never know who will harm you

vignette: María, a 59-year-old Latin American woman who has been divorced for several years, is a seasoned project manager with an extensive career in construction and real estate. Her life took a drastic turn five months ago when she was held captive by her ex-husband during a contentious divorce settlement. The trauma of that experience continues to haunt her daily. María's captivity involved being locked in various confined spaces for extended periods, often without any options to escape or seek help. This entrapment has left an indelible mark on her psyche; she now experiences intense anxiety when in closed environments, such as elevators at work or even her own home office. Her neck pain, which flared up during those days of confinement, is a constant reminder of the ordeal and often exacerbates her distress. The triggers have become deeply intertwined with María's heightened sense of threat. She feels on guard even inside her own home, where she once felt safe. The smallest things-a loud noise or an unexpected visitor-can set off a wave of panic. "I feel like I'm constantly watching my back," she says, adding that she cannot relax even when she knows she is in a safe place. Her emotional numbness has deepened over time, and María often feels dead inside, unable to connect with the joy or happiness she once experienced. She had come to believe that she used to be a happy person but now is always miserable. This despair feeds into her constant fear of harm, as she believes that you can never know who will harm you. "I'm scared because I don't trust anyone," María confides. The cycle intensifies when María engages in maladaptive strategies like magical thinking. She tells herself the event did not really happen or was not that bad to cope with the overwhelming pain. This self-blame rumination and overanalyzing of the details of her captivity only deepen her negative appraisals, making her feel more lost and hopeless. Her fear and constant alertness have led María to adopt increasingly rigid avoidance behaviors. At work, she avoids using elevators whenever possible and has become overly cautious when working on projects in confined spaces like basements or small rooms. These precautions have impacted her relationships with colleagues who find her behavior puzzling and occasionally frustrating. Her boss has noticed a decline in her productivity due to these avoidance tactics, which further reinforces María's self-blame. The false alarms she experiences are particularly distressing. On one occasion, while working on a project site, the sound of heavy machinery reminded her of the noises from her captor's tools during her captivity. She froze momentarily, unable to function until she could convince herself that she was not in danger. These moments of hypervigilance have become more frequent, making everyday tasks increasingly difficult. María's maladaptive strategies have also reinforced her negative appraisals and heightened sense of threat. Her magical thinking about the captivity diminishes only briefly before being overtaken by a flood of self-blame and overanalyzing. She is certain that if she had made different decisions during the divorce proceedings, she could have avoided the situation altogether. The cumulative effect of these symptoms has left María feeling isolated and hopeless. "I'm not sure how much longer I can keep this up," she says. What finally brought her to seek help was a realization that her work performance was declining and she was struggling to maintain any sense of normalcy in her daily life. She is most afraid of losing control completely but is also hopeful that therapy might provide some relief from the constant cycle of fear and distress. María's journey toward recovery has just begun, but it is clear that addressing these intertwined symptoms will be crucial for her well-being. Her story underscores the complex interplay between traumatic triggers, maladaptive strategies, heightened threat perception, and negative appraisals in maintaining a cycle of PTSD.
